name: Deep Space Sparkle
lede: Deep Space Sparkle is a dim, greyed teal; Wikipedia lists it among the Crayola crayon names, citing Crayola as the source.

sections.title: A crayon, not a catalogue entry
sections.body:
The name reaches our library through Wikipedia's crayon-name lists, which cite Crayola itself as the source, but the books consulted here give no date or story behind the words "space" and "sparkle" [1]. The hex value is a flat screen swatch for a crayon, not a measured pigment or a plate from a historical nomenclature [1].

The nearest unrelated record in our library is the Japanese crest color Masuhana-iro (舛花色, "Ichikawa family crest blue"), close in hex value, which our data flags only as a near match, not a shared origin [1]. Its closest look-alikes on file are [[blue-ochre]], about 2.9 units off, and [[dark-orient-blue]], with [[dark-teal-grey]] and [[dark-teal-grey]] a little further [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 1.56% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (371 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 139 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 64% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.8% of the 1,674 paintings we have from that decade (30 paintings), 2.8 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 46% of its 139 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. Its most devoted painter is Pierre-Auguste Renoir, present in 4 of 50 works here, 4.8x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 3.6x) [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].

questions.q: Where does the name Deep Space Sparkle come from?
True or false: Deep Space Sparkle shares its name origin with the Japanese color Masuhana-iro.

openers: Deep Space Sparkle is a Crayola crayon color that happens to land almost on top of a Japanese crest blue.
